meta.question: What are the obvious flaws in the Hanyu Pinyin scheme?
meta.questionZh: 《汉语拼音方案》有哪些明显的硬伤？
meta.note: English summaries are editorial translations. The full answers are in Chinese and are linked from each card.

answers.author: 匿名用户
answers.summary: A man surnamed Lü describes twenty years of fighting the same spelling: lü in dictionaries, lv on keyboards, lu on old passports, lyu on new ones. He has had to prove “I am me” to schools, banks and foreign offices.

answers.author: 欣元魂痕
answers.summary: A broad attack on the scheme’s aesthetics and regularity: r for [ɻ] but sh for [ʂ], c for [tsʰ], ao/ong, one i for two vowels. The author argues pinyin fails beauty, regularity, learnability and international use at once.

answers.author: 少学汉
answers.summary: The real flaw is the name: this is a romanization for Standard Chinese, not for Chinese as a whole. As an annotation system for the standard, it has almost no serious defects; the author explains o/uo, q/x, the two i’s, y/w and tone marking.

answers.author: Asa Ha
answers.summary: The 1956 debate already covered these objections. A romanization must satisfy accuracy, brevity, the 26-key typewriter and foreign readability; those goals contradict one another, so every fix creates a new problem.

answers.author: 玉華思賢Mijiag
answers.summary: The treatment of /y/ is the weak point: ü becomes u in ju/qu/xu, yu in yu/yue/yuan, io in jiong and yo in yong. These workarounds are harder to learn than using ü or yu consistently.

answers.author: UntPhesoca
answers.summary: A deliberately absolute position: no scheme designed with care has defects; pinyin’s design considered more cases than outsiders imagine; improving a flawless scheme is not a legitimate project.

answers.author: 日本狸猫田中裕之
answers.summary: A Japanese learner of Chinese finds pinyin useful but is confused by the dropped o in jiu: the o is reduced in speech but does not disappear, so the spelling should show it.

answers.author: DONGNANXIBEI
answers.summary: The original design wanted one letter per phoneme, hence ẑ/ĉ/ŝ/ŋ/ê/ü; in practice digraphs won. The author suggests restoring au/ung and the breve letters where useful.

answers.author: IIJEi
answers.summary: The question is what pinyin is for. It began as part of a project to replace Chinese characters, became an annotation tool, then a legal romanization and input method. Those jobs have different optimal spellings.

answers.author: Guillem
answers.summary: The theoretical irregularities are real — ü, the rarely used contractions, y/w, the treatment of apical vowels — but a national standard cannot be rewritten every time theory improves. Convention and migration cost matter more.

answers.author: Victor Yeh
answers.summary: A one-line reaction: seeing ü written as v is enough to make him angry.

answers.author: 黄艺华
answers.summary: The deepest flaw is refusing to distinguish the apical vowel in zi/ci/si/zhi/chi/shi/ri from the i in ji/qi/xi. That merger forces the redundant j/q/x series and creates gaps in the syllable table.

answers.author: qvopjhus
answers.summary: Nobody cares. Pinyin is a footbridge over a river: some deny the river, some want a concrete international bridge, some worship the old bridge, and some build their own. The essay surveys the indifference and the 2012 Shandong “revision”.

answers.author: 伊祁放勋
answers.summary: What is o supposed to sound like? In bo/po/mo/fo it behaves like uo, while uo and ou already occupy the space. The letter o has almost no independent presence.

answers.author: 气泡水在睡觉
answers.summary: A Lü in the US explains the passport/credit-card/roll-call comedy: lu, lv, lyu, and finally “just call me Louis”. The problem is not that Chinese has ü; it is that English does not.

answers.author: 王强
answers.summary: Pinyin is an unfinished building: y/w are irregular, ü is created and then hidden, iou/uei/uen lose their main vowel, and tone marking becomes awkward. The author wants the phonological principle applied consistently.

answers.author: 仙翁大桃子
answers.summary: Do “二” and “而” really sound the same? The one-line answer points at the er syllable and its spelling.

answers.author: 蓝之徒
answers.summary: The name is the problem: a scheme designed for one standardized variety is called the romanization of all Chinese. Speakers of other varieties — and even other northern dialects with ng, v or entering tones — are left outside.

answers.author: xue gy
answers.summary: Every Xue abroad has silently cursed the inventors. English speakers turn Xue into Zoo, Sue, Shoe, Shui or Jue; Turkish and German speakers do better. A legal name should not be a pronunciation test.

answers.author: 鸿烨
answers.summary: A list of twelve spelling problems — length, ü variants, bo/uo, ian/yuan, tone marks, the two i’s, y/w, ao/ong — followed by a proposed compressed alphabet.

answers.author: 梧桐
answers.summary: Pinyin is a good system, but the self-styled simplifications are indefensible: ung→ong and au→ao were justified by handwriting confusion that no longer matters. The author also objects to the six irregular zero-initial forms.

answers.author: Tanaka Yasuko
answers.summary: The scheme keeps abandoning its own principles. If ü is allowed, why not ï for the apical vowel, ž/č/š for zh/ch/sh, or ñ for ng? The author proposes a fully regular romanization with no special cases.

answers.author: 安定医院在德胜门
answers.summary: A native speaker remembers pinyin class as confusing: he already spoke the language, but had to learn arbitrary spellings and tone marks. The system is hard for both natives and learners, for different reasons.

answers.author: 苗字名前
answers.summary: The official 1956 discussion volumes show that almost every modern criticism was already on the table. The two fixed principles were Latin letters and a neat initial+final shape, which produced y/w and the “whole-syllable” readings.

answers.author: 雪凝坊
answers.summary: ü is unnecessary: only nü/nu and lü/lu need a distinction, and nyu/lyu would do the job without a special letter.

answers.author: NJMF
answers.summary: Full pinyin is slow to type; double pinyin uses two letters per syllable and is much faster. The answer explains the keyboard layout and gives a mnemonic.

answers.author: 列谿
answers.summary: The scheme was reasonable for its time. Its real problem is that its job changed: it was designed for literacy and a possible alphabetic writing system, but now it is mainly an input method, and tone cannot be typed.

answers.author: Enzojz
answers.summary: No serious flaws, except ü and the gap between letters and sounds for foreign readers. Judged only by Chinese, the design is excellent; o/bo/uo remains a genuine bug.

answers.author: 肥貓湯姆
answers.summary: The forced contractions uei→ui and iou→iu cause a chain of problems. If ü were written iu, and iou left uncontracted, much of the trouble would disappear; the i after j/q/x is also redundant.

answers.author: 高克之
answers.summary: The same letter can hide different finals: yan and gan do not rhyme, though both are written with a. Er is awkward, o is ambiguous, and y/w are inconsistent; still, pinyin is the best annotation system he has seen.

answers.author: PWang
answers.summary: Pinyin’s virtue is simplicity: it does not demand linguistic theory. Sixty years without a major revision is itself an achievement, though not proof that it cannot be improved.

answers.author: PhiLia514
answers.summary: Pinyin was never designed as an annotation system. It was meant to be a romanized writing system; when that project ended, it was repurposed for telegrams, computing and input methods. Judging it as a phonetic alphabet misses its history.

answers.author: 知乎用户MrXxK5
answers.summary: The author likes a southern variety that distinguishes sharp and rounded initials (gi, ki, hi). He proposes keeping that distinction, writing the apical vowel as ih, and using iu for ü.

answers.author: 艾迪智
answers.summary: The letter-level debates matter less than the human cost: Chinese people adopt English names because foreigners cannot read pinyin names. A better romanization would help both sides.

answers.author: Ha Neul
answers.summary: Little is wrong beyond details: use iu for ü, keep iou uncontracted, and write iong/ong as iung/ung so the correspondences are visible.

answers.author: 啪栏杆
answers.summary: A detailed history of the 1955–58 drafts: the first draft used y for ü, j for the glide, g/k/h for j/q/x, and kept au/ung. The final scheme adopted the second revision instead, mixing Northern Latinization and Gwoyeu Romatzyh.

answers.author: 天涯之夏
answers.summary: Restore au/iau/ung/iung, undo the iou/uei contractions, and write ü as yu to avoid the diaeresis.

answers.author: McLarenMP4-4
answers.summary: No obvious flaws; it is the best available scheme. It passed every official body, became ISO 7098 and is written into the language law. The author quotes Zhou Youguang’s account of the 1950s debates at length.

answers.author: 徐伟
answers.summary: The author, who has designed several romanizations, argues that tone marking is the main defect: the marks are hard to type and often omitted. He proposes a Zhuang-style letter-based tone system and a more phonemic spelling.
